# The Heat Is a Design Problem: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

For most of the twentieth century, cities treated heat as weather—something to be endured rather than designed around. That posture has become untenable. The 1995 Chicago heat wave killed more than 700 people, most of them elderly and isolated in apartments that never cooled down. The 2003 European heat wave killed an estimated 70,000. Phoenix now records hundreds of heat deaths annually, and cities from Portland to Paris have suffered lethal heat events that would have been statistically impossible a century ago. The central argument of this essay is that extreme heat is not merely a climate problem but a *design* problem: the way cities are built—their surfaces, their streets, their housing, their transportation systems—determines who suffers and who survives. Cities can be retrofitted for heat, but every intervention carries costs and tradeoffs, and the hardest question is not technical but political: who bears those costs, and who reaps the benefits?

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

Trees remain the most effective and best-loved tool for cooling a city. Shade can reduce the perceived temperature of a street by tens of degrees, and evapotranspiration—the process by which trees release water vapor—cools the surrounding air measurably. The effects are not evenly distributed, however. In most American cities, tree canopy maps overlay almost perfectly with historical maps of redlining and wealth: leafy, affluent neighborhoods can be several degrees cooler than low-income neighborhoods a few miles away. In Baltimore, some neighborhoods enjoy more than 40 percent canopy cover while others have less than 10 percent.

The most celebrated example of deliberate tree-based cooling is Medellín, Colombia. Beginning in 2016, the city built thirty "green corridors"—strips of trees, shrubs, and vines along roads and waterways—reducing local temperatures by roughly 2 degrees Celsius and creating pleasant public space in the bargain. The program cost relatively little because it was integrated into existing infrastructure. Singapore, facing a tropical climate, has pursued a similar strategy with "vertical greenery" and a national tree-planting campaign dating back to the 1960s.

But trees carry real tradeoffs. They require water—in Phoenix and other arid cities, a mature tree can consume hundreds of gallons weekly, forcing a genuine calculation between water scarcity and heat relief. Trees can buckle sidewalks, block sightlines, aggravate allergies, and, if poorly maintained, drop limbs. And there is a subtler problem researchers call "green gentrification": when a neighborhood is greened, it becomes more desirable, property values rise, and the very residents who endured the heat of a treeless district may be priced out of the shade they helped advocate for. Cities that plant trees without anti-displacement policies—rent stabilization, affordable housing mandates, community land trusts—may simply relocate the heat vulnerability elsewhere.

## Street Design: The Surfaces Beneath Our Feet

If trees are the canopy, streets are the body of the heat problem. Asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight all day and radiate it back all night, which is why urban heat islands are most dangerous after sunset, when the body needs to recover. Street design can attack this in two ways: changing the materials and changing the geometry.

Los Angeles has experimented with "cool pavements"—light-colored coatings that reflect rather than absorb sunlight—on dozens of streets, measuring surface temperature reductions of 10 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit. The results are instructive in their complications. Because the coating reflects sunlight, pedestrians standing on the street can actually *feel* hotter, as radiation bounces up rather than sinking into the asphalt. Cool pavements work best where pedestrians are shaded or elevated; they are not a substitute for shade. New York's "Cool Roofs" program, by contrast, paints rooftops white, which cools the building below and the air above without baking pedestrians.

Geometry matters as much as material. Narrow streets, arcades, and buildings set close together—as in the old cores of Seville, Athens, or Fez—create shade and channel breezes. The Haussmann boulevards of Paris, with their stone facades and tree-lined medians, are often criticized for their imperial rigidity, but their deep, shaded sidewalks and uniform height create a remarkably comfortable microclimate. Modern street design can borrow these lessons: orienting streets to prevailing winds, requiring awnings and colonnades, and widening sidewalks to make room for shade trees and benches. The tradeoff is space and speed. Every lane given over to shade and pedestrians is a lane taken from cars, and in a city like Los Angeles, that is a political fight, not a technical one.

## Housing: The Front Line of Heat Death

Most heat deaths happen indoors, in homes that trap heat. The 1995 Chicago disaster killed people in top-floor apartments with black tar roofs and no air conditioning, in buildings where residents feared opening windows because of crime. The lesson is that housing policy is heat policy.

Several interventions matter. Building codes can require reflective or "green" roofs, high-albedo walls, and above all insulation—insulation keeps heat out in summer as well as in during winter. Cities can mandate or subsidize air conditioning, but this creates a vicious cycle: A/C dumps heat into the street while straining a fossil-fueled grid. The more durable solution is passive cooling: cross-ventilation, exterior shading, thermal mass, and windows that actually open. Singapore's Housing Development Board designs public housing blocks with orientation and void decks that channel airflow; the buildings are cooler by design, not by machinery.

The tradeoff is cost and speed. Retrofitting millions of existing apartments is enormously expensive, and landlords often pass costs to tenants. Renters face a cruel asymmetry: they cannot install a heat pump, paint a roof, or replace single-pane windows, and in many jurisdictions they have no legal right to a maximum temperature, even as many cities guarantee a minimum temperature in winter. New York and other cities have begun debating a "maximum heat law" for rental housing—an idea that would have been unthinkable a generation ago and that illustrates the shift in thinking: cooling is becoming a utility, not a luxury.
